title: The taxi with no address

beats.say: Imagine hopping into a taxi and saying only, take me somewhere good. What happens?

The driver circles the city, guessing, while the meter runs. You may end up at the wrong place. A coding agent does the same with the words fix the bug. It reads the whole project, guesses which bug you mean, and decides for itself when it is done.
Now give the address, the roads to avoid, and how you will know you arrived. Fewer wrong turns, a smaller bill, and a result you can check.

show.title: A good ask names
items: The address: what outcome you want
The roads to avoid: what must not change
The proof you arrived: how to check

check.q: Why is a short prompt like fix the bug expensive?
opts: The agent charges per word you type
The agent fills the gaps by exploring and guessing, using turns and tokens
The agent refuses vague prompts
check.why: Every gap you leave becomes reading, guessing and choosing its own definition of done, which costs turns and tokens and may still be wrong.

work: Rewrite one vague prompt you used this week so it names the outcome and where to look.
Before sending a prompt, ask yourself what the agent would have to guess.

title: Five parts of a good prompt

beats.say: Which five parts turn a vague request into one an agent can finish in a single go?

Goal is the outcome: European amounts like twelve comma fifty must parse as twelve point five. Context is where to look: the parse amount function in ingest dot py, and the vendor notes saying German and French files use a decimal comma.

Constraints say what must not change: keep the US format one thousand two hundred thirty four point fifty working, add no dependencies, leave load dot py alone. Verification names the tests that must pass, plus a new one for the European thousands style, one dot two three four comma five zero.

show.title: Constraints and verification
items: No new dependencies; do not touch load.py

beats.say: Output is what you want back: a plan first, then a three line summary and the diff.

check.q: Which part tells the agent how to know the change worked?
opts: Context
Constraints
Verification
check.why: Verification names the tests or checks that must pass, so the agent can run them and correct itself.

work: Write a five-line prompt template with goal, context, constraints, verification and output.
Name the exact tests or commands that prove your next change worked.

title: Why verification and constraints matter

beats.say: Why does an agent without a test stop at code that merely looks right?

Because nothing tells it otherwise. With a failing test it runs the test, reads the error, and tries again until it passes. That loop is self-correction. Without one, plausible is the only bar, and you find the mistake later in review.

Gaps also cost money. Each unclear spot becomes extra file reads, which means extra turns and tokens. Skip constraints and it may touch load dot py or add a library. Watch the test itself: say whether the agent may change tests, or it may bend the check instead of the code.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Every gap becomes extra reading, turns and tokens
No constraints: it may edit load.py or add a library
Say if tests may be changed, or it may bend the check
Guess wrong about which bug, and the whole run is wasted

check.q: An agent fixes the bug, but you gave no test and no constraints. What is the most likely risk?
opts: The code looks plausible but is unverified and may touch things you wanted left alone
The agent will refuse to edit any file
The agent will use fewer tokens than normal
check.why: Without verification the agent stops when the code looks plausible, and without constraints it may change files or add dependencies you wanted untouched.

work: Add a line to prompts saying whether tests may be edited.
List the files and dependencies that are off limits before asking for a change.

title: How much prompt is enough

beats.say: Should every prompt carry all five parts?
No. A quick question needs only goal and context. Writing a long brief for a one line answer costs you more than it saves.
For any change, never drop verification. It costs a few lines, and it lets the agent check itself instead of you rereading every diff.

chip.text: Move the checking to the agent

beats.say: When you cannot define the fix yet, ask for a plan first. Reviewing a plan is cheap, and it catches a wrong guess before the agent spends turns building it. Turn your best prompts into team templates.

check.q: You cannot yet say exactly what the fix should be. What is the cheapest sensible prompt?
opts: Fix the bug and surprise me
Give goal and context, and ask for a plan before any edits
Skip the goal and ask for a diff only
check.why: A plan is cheap to review and exposes a wrong guess before the agent spends turns and tokens building it.

work: Create a short team template with goal, context, constraints, verification and output.
Ask for a plan first on any change where you cannot state the fix in one sentence.

title: Blueprint before concrete

beats.say: Would you let a builder pour concrete before showing you the blueprint?
Working with an AI coding assistant is similar. Plan mode means it reads your code and writes a short plan first, without changing a single file.
You read ten lines in a minute. If the approach is wrong, you say so before two hundred lines exist. Fixing a sketch is cheap. Fixing a built wall is not.

show.title: Cost of fixing a wrong approach

beats.say: And if it starts building the wrong thing, interrupt at once. A quick word now beats a long argument later.

check.q: Why ask for a plan before a big change?
opts: It makes the code run faster
You can catch a wrong approach before much code is written
It removes the need to review the final code
check.why: A plan takes a minute to read and costs nothing to change, while a wrong approach discovered after hundreds of lines is expensive to undo.

work: Before your next multi-file change, ask for a plan and read it fully.
Write down one thing you would have missed without the plan.

title: Plan, then steer with precise follow-ups

beats.say: What does one minute of reading buy you?
In plan mode, Claude explores the code and proposes steps, maybe ten lines, and edits nothing. You read it and spot a wrong approach before two hundred lines are written.

Then steer with specific follow ups. Say, option two, but keep the function signature unchanged. Or ask, what breaks if a value is one thousand two hundred thirty four, with no decimal part? Or, do two commits: tests first, then the fix.

show.title: Good follow-ups
items: What breaks for a value like 1,234?
Two commits: tests first, then fix

beats.say: Each reply narrows the plan. Only then do you approve the edit.

check.q: Which follow-up best steers a plan without throwing it away?
opts: Try again
Option 2, but keep the function signature unchanged
Make it better
check.why: It picks a direction and names a firm constraint. Vague replies give the assistant nothing concrete to change.

work: After reading a plan, reply with one choice and one constraint.
Ask what breaks for an edge-case input before approving.

title: Interrupting mid-edit and plan blind spots

beats.say: Claude is halfway through an edit and heading the wrong way. What do you do?
Press Escape. That interrupts it immediately, and you type a short correction. Waiting means it keeps building on the wrong assumption, and every extra file is something you must undo.
Plans also have blind spots. A plan that sounds fine may ignore edge cases, like a number with no decimal part. So ask what would break, and name the cases you fear.

show.title: Plan blind spots
items: Edge cases like 1,234 with no decimals

beats.say: Tests first, then the fix, gives you a check. The new test should fail before the fix and pass after. If it passes early, the test proves nothing.

check.q: In a tests-first commit, the new test already passes before the fix. What does that suggest?
opts: The fix is unnecessary and perfect
The test does not capture the bug
Claude should keep going
check.why: A test that never failed cannot prove the fix worked, so it probably misses the real bug.

work: Press Esc the moment you see a wrong direction instead of waiting for it to finish.
Ask for the failing test to be run and shown before the fix.

title: When planning pays and when it doesn't

beats.say: When is a plan not worth reading?

show.text: Plan when it's costly to be wrong

beats.say: Planning costs minutes. A wrong approach costs more as the change grows: rewriting two hundred lines, reviewing a huge diff, untangling a merged mess. So plan when the change is bigger than a one-line fix or touches shared code.
Skip it for a typo or a rename you can describe in one sentence. A plan there is ceremony.
Prefer small commits too. Tests first, then the fix, makes each step reviewable and revertible. Steering early is risk control: you catch errors when they are cheapest.

check.q: Which change most justifies plan mode?
opts: Fixing a typo in a comment
Renaming one local variable
Changing a shared formatting function used in many places
check.why: Shared code multiplies the cost of a wrong approach, so a short plan is worth the minute it takes to read.

work: Set a team rule: plan first for anything beyond a one-line fix or touching shared code.
Ask for tests-first commits so each change can be reviewed and reverted alone.

title: The plumber who has never seen your house

beats.say: Imagine hiring the world's best plumber, but not telling them which tap leaks. What happens?
The plumber is brilliant, but has never seen your house. They don't know your pipes are old, or that you tried tape last year. Clever tricks can't replace those facts.

chip.text: Skill is not knowledge of your house

beats.say: AI coding tools are the same. They know a huge amount about code. They know nothing about your company, your data, or your past mistakes.
So the best sentences in a request are facts only you know. Say which tap leaks, point at the file, and paste the exact error message.

show.sub: Name the file. Paste the error.

check.q: Why does a very capable AI still produce a wrong fix?
opts: It lacks facts that only you know
It needs a more polite request
It forgets how to code
It works better with shorter requests
check.why: The model's skill is general. Your business rules, history and setup are not visible to it, so you must say them.

work: Before your next request, write down one fact only your team knows and add it.
Name the exact file or error instead of describing the problem loosely.

title: Four facts a model cannot find

beats.say: Which four kinds of facts can a model never find on its own?

First, business rules. The EU shop writes twelve fifty as twelve comma five zero. The US shop writes one thousand two hundred fifty as one comma two five zero. Without the rule, the model guesses, and totals come out wrong.

Second, scale. The job runs daily on fifty million rows, so per-row Python regex would crawl. Third, history. Finance already rejected rounding. Fourth, environment. The cluster runs Spark three point three, so newer functions fail.

show.title: Scale, history, environment
items: 50 million rows daily: no per-row regex
Cluster is Spark 3.3: no newer functions

beats.say: Then attach evidence. Point at files with the at sign, paste the exact error and the command, and drag in a screenshot of the wrong total.

show.title: Evidence beats description
show.text:
fix the total in @jobs/daily_sales.py
run: spark-submit jobs/daily_sales.py
error: pasted exactly, plus dashboard screenshot

check.q: Which sentence adds the most value to a request about a slow daily job?
opts: Please be very careful and think hard
It runs daily on 50 million rows, so avoid per-row Python
You are a world-class data engineer
Make it fast
check.why: Scale is a fact the model cannot discover, and it changes which solutions are acceptable. The other lines are tone or vague.

work: Add a one-line scale fact (rows, frequency) to every performance request.
Paste the exact error and the exact command that produced it, not a summary.
Attach a screenshot when a dashboard shows the wrong number.

title: When context goes wrong

beats.say: Why did the model write a perfect fix for the wrong problem?

show.sub: Context was off, not the model

beats.say: Usually your description drifted from reality. Describe a file from memory and the model trusts your memory, not the code. Point at it with the at sign instead, so it reads the real thing.

chip.text: Point at the source of truth

beats.say: Trim an error and you may cut the one line that names the cause. Paste the whole message and the exact command. But redact passwords and customer data first, because pasted text leaves your machine.

show.title: Pasting safely
items: Whole error, not a trimmed copy

beats.say: More is not always better. Pointing at a whole folder buries the key fact. Give the two files that matter and the easy-to-miss rule. And state facts as facts: a wrong rule produces confidently wrong code.

show.sub: A wrong fact gives confident wrong code

check.q: You paste only the last line of a long stack trace. What is the main risk?
opts: The model will refuse to answer
You may have cut the line that names the real cause
The trace becomes too accurate
The command will run twice
check.why: The root cause often sits earlier in the trace. Trimming removes evidence the model cannot recover on its own.

work: Replace described files with at references in your next three prompts.
Create a redaction habit: scrub keys, tokens and customer rows before pasting.
Check each stated rule is still true before you hand it over.

title: Facts last, tricks expire

beats.say: Should you spend a week polishing prompt tricks, or writing down what your team already knows?

show.sub: Where does the effort pay back?

beats.say: Clever phrasing is brittle. It shifts with every model version. Facts like Spark three point three, or no rounding, stay true for years, so they earn a permanent place.
So store durable facts once, in a project memory file the tool loads every session, instead of retyping them. Keep it short, because every line costs tokens and competes for attention.
Better still, turn hard rules into tests. A check that fails on rounded totals beats a sentence asking nicely. Skip heavy context for tiny one-off edits, where it only adds noise.

show.title: Choose the right tool
items: Hard rule: enforce with a test
Tiny edit: one line, no extra context

check.q: Finance forbids rounding totals. What is the strongest way to protect that rule?
opts: Repeat it in capital letters in every prompt
Add a test that fails when totals are rounded
Trust the model to remember it
Describe it in a long essay
check.why: A test enforces the rule regardless of who or what writes the code. Prompt text only asks; a test checks.

work: Move your three most repeated facts into a short project memory file.
Convert one business rule into an automated test or data check.
Prune context that no longer applies each quarter.

title: Brief the AI like a builder

beats.say: Why does a clever AI helper still hand you the wrong thing? Usually because the brief was vague.

show.sub: The helper guesses what you meant

beats.say: Think of a builder. Say fix the house, and they might repaint the kitchen. Say the tap leaks, show me the leak first, then fix only the tap, and you get what you wanted.

chip.text: Prove it, fix it, touch nothing else

beats.say: Good prompts work the same way. Ask for a test that proves the problem. Let the helper ask you questions first. Say how short the answer should be. And say what not to touch.

show.title: Four habits
items: Set a size for the answer

beats.say: Small, clear jobs beat one giant vague one.

check.q: Which request is closest to a good brief?
opts: Make it better
Fix everything in this project
Show the bug with a failing test, then fix only that function
Update the code and also write docs and rename the files
check.why: It names one job, proves the problem first and limits the scope. The others are vague or bundle unrelated work.

work: Rewrite your last vague prompt so it names one job and one result.
Add one sentence saying what the AI must not touch.
Keep a note of prompts that worked and reuse them.

title: The five patterns, step by step

beats.say: How do you know an AI fix really fixed the bug?

show.text: How do you know it worked?

beats.say: Use test first. Step one, the AI writes a test that fails because of the bug. Step two, it runs the test and you see red. Step three, it changes the code until the test goes green. Step four, you confirm the test file was never edited. Now green means something.
Add a bound. Ask for only the changed function, or an answer under eight lines. A two hundred line reply takes minutes to read and costs more tokens. Eight lines you can check in seconds.
Finally, ask it to put up to three questions to you first. Three answers cost you a minute. A wrong guess can cost a whole rewrite.

check.q: In test first, what is the point of running the test before fixing?
opts: It warms up the test runner
It proves the test really fails on the bug
It makes the answer shorter
It lets the AI edit the test later
check.why: A test that never failed proves nothing. Seeing it red first shows it catches the bug, so green later is real evidence.

work: Next bug fix, ask for a failing test and make it show the red run.
Add a line limit to prompts where you only need a small change.
Use interview me whenever a task has two plausible meanings.

title: Where these patterns break

beats.say: Your test passes. So why might the bug still be there?

Because the model can cheat. Under pressure it may weaken the test instead of fixing the code. That is why the prompt says do not change the test. Also check the test failed for the right reason, not a typo or a missing import.

chip.text: Lock the test, read the failure message

beats.say: Negative rules matter too. Without do not refactor unrelated code, a one line fix can become a forty file diff nobody can review.
And sessions drift. Every old message stays in context, so after a topic change the model may lean on stale details, and each turn costs more. Run slash clear between unrelated tasks.

show.title: Session drift
items: Stale details leak into new work

check.q: A fix makes the test pass, but the diff shows the test assertion was loosened. What happened?
opts: Normal refactoring
The model changed the target instead of the code
The test runner is broken
Nothing, green is green
check.why: Editing the test to pass defeats its purpose. Forbid test changes and review the test diff separately.

work: Always read the test diff, not only the code diff.
Add a rule against unrelated refactors to your standard prompt.
Run slash clear before starting a new topic.

title: When to skip the patterns

beats.say: Should every prompt use every pattern? No. Knowing when to skip them is the senior skill.

show.sub: Use them where they pay back

beats.say: Interview me costs a round trip. For a one line rename, just do it. Use it when a wrong guess means rework. Test first needs a runnable test setup. For a throwaway prototype, it is overhead.

show.title: Skip when
items: No test harness: skip test first

beats.say: Bounding output saves tokens but can hide reasoning. For a design decision, ask for the trade-offs, then trim. A reviewer-style explanation helps, but it is the model grading itself. Your continuous integration pipeline stays the real gate.
At team scale, put repeated rules, like no unrelated refactors, in a shared project instructions file so nobody retypes them. Split big jobs into one task per session.

show.title: Scale it
items: Shared rules file for the team

check.q: Which situation is the weakest fit for interview me?
opts: Ambiguous feature with two possible designs
Renaming one variable in one file
Migrating a data model with unclear ownership
Choosing between two APIs
check.why: A trivial, unambiguous change gains nothing from questions and just adds a round trip.

work: Move your repeated prompt rules into a shared project instructions file.
Keep CI checks as the merge gate, whatever the AI says about its diff.
Split large requests into separate sessions, one task each.
